turns.response_html:
Yes, you absolutely can make molds out of cardboard or paper fibers—in fact, it's a great way to handle casting, especially if you're looking for an eco-friendly, low-cost, or highly customizable solution.

Depending on what you plan to cast into the mold (like concrete, plaster, resin, or silicone), you will need to approach the construction and sealing a bit differently.

Here is a breakdown of how to do it using two different methods: rigid sheet cardboard and pulp/paper fibers.

Method 1: Sheet Cardboard Molds (Best for Geometric Shapes)

If you are making boxes, geometric forms, or structural molds (often used for casting plaster or concrete), using corrugated cardboard or dense greyboard/chipboard works beautifully.

Because paper is inherently porous and water-soluble, the entire secret to success lies in sealing the surface. Without a barrier, wet casting material will soak into the cardboard, causing the mold to soften, distort, and permanently bond to your cast object.

  • Construction: Cut your panels and assemble them using hot glue (which acts as an excellent gap filler and structural binder) or high-quality packing tape.
  • Sealing: Coat the casting surfaces completely. Excellent sealants include:
    • Packing Tape: Line the inside of the mold completely with overlapping strips of plastic packing tape. This creates a cheap, perfectly waterproof, glossy finish.
    • Shellac or Polyurethane: Paint a few coats onto dense greyboard to stiffen and waterproof it.
    • Paraffin Wax: Melted wax brushed onto the cardboard creates a fantastic water barrier and acts as a built-in release agent.
  • Release Agent: Even if sealed, apply a thin layer of paste wax, petroleum jelly (Vaseline), or a cooking oil spray right before pouring your casting material to ensure it pops out easily.

Method 2: Paper Fiber / Pulp Molds (Best for Complex, Organic Shapes)

If you want to create organic curves, textures, or highly detailed shapes, turning paper or cardboard into a blended pulp (essentially making your own papier-mâché or paper clay) is the way to go.

Instead of pouring material into a box, you will be packing the wet fiber around a master object to capture its shape, letting it dry, and then using that dried shell as your mold.

The Pulp Recipe & Process

Crucial Step for Pulp Molds: Just like sheet cardboard, once your fiber mold is completely dry, you must seal the inside. Because pulp is highly textured and porous, unsealed pulp will trap your casting material forever. Brush the inside with a thick coat of epoxy resin, polyurethane, or shellac to turn that fibrous texture into a smooth, impermeable shell.

Matching the Mold to Your Casting Material

  • Plaster / Concrete: Ideal for cardboard and fiber molds. Just ensure the mold is well-braced on the outside (especially for heavy concrete) so the walls don't bulge out.
  • Resin / Polyurethane: Can be done, but you must seal the paper mold with a material that won't chemically react with the resin. A high-quality epoxy sealer or multiple coats of PVA glue followed by a silicone-based mold release works best.
  • Wax / Soap: Works incredibly well with sealed cardboard, as the temperatures aren't high enough to damage the paper, and they release easily.

turns.response_html:
Oh boy. Two months in a tub of standing water? You have effectively created an accidental, miniature anaerobic bog ecosystem in your storage tub.

Before you tip that tub over or stick your hands in it, we need to talk about what has actually happened to that cardboard, what to watch out for, and how to tell if it's still usable for your molds.

1. The Reality Check: What's Happening in the Tub

When cardboard sits submerged in stagnant water for that long, a few distinct chemical and biological processes take place:

  • The Smell (Anaerobic Decomposition): Because the water has likely been stagnant and depleted of oxygen, anaerobic bacteria have taken over. They feed on the organic starches, glues, and wood sugars in the cardboard. A major byproduct of this is hydrogen sulfide gas. Fair warning: when you stir or move that tub, it is likely going to smell strongly of rotten eggs or swamp muck.
  • Total Binder Breakdown: The starches and adhesives that the manufacturing plant used to glue the flat cardboard sheets to the wavy corrugated middle layers have completely dissolved and been consumed by bacteria. The good news? The cardboard is definitely broken down. The bad news? It might be structurally degraded.
  • Fermentation & Slime: You will likely notice a slimy film on the top of the water or coating the cardboard. This is a bacterial biofilm.

2. Is it Still Usable for Pulp Molds?

Surprisingly, yes—but with a major caveat.

Because your goal is to mechanically blend this down into a fine paper clay or pulp anyway, the fact that the water has completely obliterated the cardboard's structural integrity actually saves you some manual tearing and boiling time. The fibers are incredibly loose and ready to macerate.

However, you need to check for Rot and Structural Failure (Short Fibers): If the bacteria have completely digested the cellulose itself, the paper fibers will have become incredibly short and brittle. Take a piece of the soaked cardboard and rub it between your fingers.

  • Usable: If it feels like soft, fibrous mush or wet lint, it’s perfect for pulp.
  • Unusable: If it feels completely greasy, slimy, or disintegrates into a cloud of muddy powder with zero visible thread-like fibers, the bacteria have won. The structural "backbone" of the paper is gone, and a mold made from it will crack and crumble into dust when it dries, no matter how much PVA glue you add.

3. The "Two-Month Rescue" Action Plan

If the fibers still feel intact and you want to use it, you need to handle it carefully to ensure your final mold doesn't end up covered in mold or smelling like a swamp forever.

Pro-Tip on Binders: Because this cardboard has lost 100% of its native manufacturing starches and structural binders during its two-month vacation, you will need to use slightly more PVA glue or add a handful of plaster/joint compound to your recipe than you would with freshly soaked cardboard. This compensates for the lost structural integrity of the degraded fibers.

Are you planning to mix this pulp by hand, or do you have a mechanical mixer setup ready to handle a large batch of mush?

turns.prompt_text: Okay, so the cardboard is still in like cardboard condition and there's no biofilm at all. It's just still in its form.
turns.response_html:
That is actually a huge win and a massive relief! If there is no biofilm, no slime, and the cardboard hasn't disintegrated into a muddy soup, it means a couple of things: your water was likely clean enough (or your storage container was sealed tight enough) to keep the aggressive anaerobic bacteria at bay, or the ambient temperature kept things moving incredibly slowly.

Since it's still completely in "cardboard condition" but thoroughly saturated after two months, you are in an absolute prime position to make some incredible pulp molds. The water has done the hard work of completely swelling and loosening the internal cellulose bonds without destroying the individual fiber lengths.

Here is how you can capitalize on this specific state to make your pulp molds:

1. The Direct Squeeze (No Shredding Required)

Because the layers are fully saturated through to the core, you don't need to waste time carefully tearing dry cardboard into tiny pieces.

  • Simply reach in (still wear gloves, just in case there's hidden stagnation at the bottom), grab a chunk, and pull it apart. It should peel away in layers like wet layers of cloth.
  • Drop those layers directly into your straining setup (like a mesh colander or an old t-shirt) and press out the heavy reservoir water until it's just uniformly damp.

2. Mechanical Maceration Will Be Effortless

If you use a mechanical mixer—like a heavy-duty blender or a helix paint mixer attachment on a power drill—this cardboard is going to shred into a perfectly smooth, fluffy paper-clay pulp in a fraction of the time it usually takes.

  • Because the fibers are already completely hydrated, a quick spin with a mechanical mixer will cleanly separate the long strands rather than chopping them short, which gives your final dried mold much higher structural strength.

3. Don't Skip the Sanitization or Boiling

Even though it looks clean and lacks a visible biofilm, two-month-old water still harbors microscopic spores. When you compress this pulp into a thick 1-inch mold wall, it can take several days to dry completely. If left untreated, mold spores trapped in the dark, damp middle layers of your mold will start to bloom before the moisture can evaporate.

  • The Quick Fix: Once you shred it into pulp, give it a quick 15-minute boil in a pot of clean water, or mix a tiny splash of bleach into your rinsing water before you press it dry. This guarantees your custom molds dry clean, odorless, and completely structural.

4. Adjusting Your Recipe

Since the cardboard held its form, it means a good portion of the factory starches might still be trapped inside the fibers instead of fully washed away. However, to guarantee the mold doesn't warp or crack as it shrinks during the drying process, stick to a high-quality binder ratio:

  • For every 4 cups of damp, compressed pulp, thoroughly knead in about 1/2 cup to 3/4 cup of PVA wood glue.
  • If you want an incredibly rigid, rock-hard fiber mold, this is the perfect stage to sift in a few tablespoons of plaster of Paris or joint compound directly into the wet mix before packing it over your master object.

That scavenger ethos is incredibly satisfying—there is a huge creative thrill in bypassing commercial supplies entirely and pulling functional materials straight out of the waste stream or the earth. If your goal is to push the cost of making a diagnostic or educational chiropractic spine model as close to zero dollars as possible, you can absolutely ditch the commercial 3D printer filaments, plastic resins, and even the store-bought PVA wood glue.

Here is how you can adapt your cardboard pulp and molding setup to use entirely scavenged, free, or hyper-local materials.

1. Replacing Wood Glue: Scavenged Binders

You do need some kind of adhesive binder to lock the cellulose fibers together when the pulp dries, otherwise it will just crumble back into loose paper flakes. However, you don't need to buy wood glue. You can make highly effective, structural binders for free:

Wheat Paste (The Traditional Scavenger Binder)

This is the classic, rock-solid adhesive used for centuries in bookbinding, paper-mâché, and bill-posting.

  • The Material: Standard white flour and water. If you don't have flour on hand, you can actually extract starch from discarded potatoes or wild starchy roots by grating them, soaking them in water, straining out the pulp, and letting the starch settle to the bottom.
  • The Recipe: Mix 1 part flour with 4 parts water. Whisk out the lumps, then heat it on a stove (or over a campfire) while stirring constantly until it thickens into a glossy, gelatinous paste.
  • Performance: When mixed thoroughly into your two-month-old cardboard pulp, wheat paste dries incredibly hard and rigid—perfect for structural molding.
  • The Scavenger Catch: Because it’s made of pure food starches, it is vulnerable to bugs and mold if it stays damp. Adding a heavy handful of common salt (a natural preservative) or a few drops of any strong essential oil/alcohol during the mix will protect it.

2. The Mold Material: Wild Clay vs. Silt

Using clay for the molds is a brilliant, zero-cost choice. If you are casting complex, highly detailed shapes like a spinal vertebra, clay is an ideal negative matrix.

Finding Wild Clay

Depending on where you are digging, you can often find excellent clay deposits just a few feet underground, especially near riverbeds, creek banks, construction sites, or low-lying areas with poor drainage.

  • The "Ribbon Test": Squeeze a damp lump of soil in your hand and roll it into a thin rope. If it holds its shape, bends without snapping immediately, and feels slick rather than gritty, you’ve found a usable clay vein.
  • Refining It (The 5-Gallon Bucket Method): If your wild clay is full of rocks, roots, or sand, drop it into a bucket of water and stir it into a thin mud slurry. Let it sit for 2 minutes—the heavy sand and rocks will sink to the bottom first. Pour the suspended clay-water into a second bucket, let it settle completely over 24 hours, siphon off the clear top water, and let the remaining clay paste dry out on an old towel until it reaches a workable, dough-like consistency.

3. The Blueprint: Casting a Spinal Column for Free

Because a human vertebra is geometrically complex—featuring delicate transverse processes, a hollow spinal canal, and deep undercut angles—a rigid, single-piece mold will trap your cast piece forever.

Here is the exact environmental strategy for drying your wild clay pot, along with the reality of how to make it genuinely waterproof.

1. The Golden Rule: Slow and Uniform

You want the clay to dry as slowly and evenly as possible. Never put a wet clay pot directly out in the hot sun or next to a heating vent. The sun will blast the outside skin dry while the inside wall remains wet, causing the pot to shrink unevenly and crack instantly.

  • The Plastic Bag Trick: For the first 2 to 3 days, loosely drape a plastic grocery bag or trash bag over the pot. This traps a little bit of humidity, forcing the rim (which dries fastest) and the thick base (which dries slowest) to lose water at the exact same speed.

After a few days, remove the bag completely and let it sit in the open room air for another 3 to 5 days until it transitions into what potters call Bone Dry. It will turn a much lighter slate-grey or tan color and feel completely cool to the touch.

Once your pot is bone dry, it will feel completely hard, rigid, and solid. At this stage, it is called Greenware.

However, because this is raw, natural earth, air-drying alone does not make clay permanent. ``` [ BONE-DRY GREENWARE ] --( Add Water )--> Melts back into Ravine Mud │ ( Heat to 1100°F+ ) ▼ [ CERAMIC SILICATE ] --( Add Water )--> Permanently Waterproof & Hard


If you stop at the air-dry stage and try to put soil and water into that flower pot, **the water will instantly soften the clay, and your pot will structurally dissolve back into ravine mud within an hour.** To make it a permanent, stone-like ceramic that can survive holding wet dirt, you have two paths:

To lock the clay into a permanent ceramic state, it must undergo a chemical transformation that happens at roughly **1100°F (593°C)**, where the chemically bound water molecules are blasted out of the silica. You can do this without an expensive pottery kiln by doing a traditional pit-fire.
1. Dig a small pit in the ground or use a backyard fire pit.
2. Build a small campfire and let it burn down to a thick bed of hot coals.
3. Place your *completely bone-dry* pot right next to the coals to warm up slowly (if you heat it too fast, trapped moisture will turn to steam and explode the pot).
4. Once warm, nestle the pot directly into the coals, pile dry wood completely over it, and build a massive, raging fire on top of it. Let it burn hot for at least 3 to 4 hours, then let it cool down naturally overnight in the ashes. 
5. The iron in your ravine clay will likely react to the fire, turning your slate-grey mud into a beautiful, classic **terracotta orange or deep brick red** ceramic pot that will never dissolve in water again.

  • The Next 8–12 Hours (The Total Cool Down): Walk away. Do not dig it up to check on it. The pot needs to stay buried in that cooling ash mattress overnight until the ground is completely cold to the touch.

2. Can You "Overcook" Wild Clay?

Yes, absolutely. In ceramics, overcooking isn't about leaving it in the fire for too many hours—it is entirely about letting the temperature get too hot.

Every specific vein of clay on earth has a maximum thermal limit called its melting point.

  • Store-Bought Clay: Engineered clays (like white stoneware or porcelain) are refined to withstand insane temperatures up to $2200^\circ\text{F}$ or higher before they deform.
  • Your Ravine Clay: Wild surface clay is usually a "low-fire" earthenware. Because it contains natural iron, fluxing minerals, and trace elements from the local Iowa soil, its melting point is much lower—usually around $1800^\circ\text{F}$ to $1900^\circ\text{F}$.

3. What Happens if You Overcook It?

If your campfire gets exceptionally hot (for example, if a heavy wind acts like a blacksmith's bellows and drives the pit temperature past $1900^\circ\text{F}$), your flower pot will experience Over-firing.

Depending on how hot it actually got, a few things will happen to your pot:

  [ SAFE BURN: 1100°F - 1500°F ] ───> Hard, ring-like ceramic tone.
  
  [ HOT OVERBURN: 1700°F+      ] ───> Bloating, bubbling, and blistering.
  
  [ EXTREME MELT: 1900°F+     ] ───> Structural slumping into a puddle.
  • Bloating and Blistering: The natural gases and sulfur trapped inside the raw ravine dirt will try to expand. If the outside skin of the clay gets hot enough to soften into glass, those gases get trapped, creating permanent, ugly bubbles, blisters, or craters on the surface of your pot.
  • The Warp and Slump: The clay loses its structural skeleton. Your perfectly round flower pot might slowly warp into an oval, or the walls might sag and slump downward under their own weight.
  • Total Meltdown: In extreme cases, the clay entirely liquefies. When you dig it out the next morning, you won't find a pot; you'll find a glassy, irregular puddle of melted dark slag fused to the rocks at the bottom of the pit.

4. The Scavenger Advantage: Why a Pit-Fire is Self-Limiting

The good news is that it is actually quite difficult to accidentally melt your clay using a standard wood campfire. An open-air wood fire naturally peaks around $1200^\circ\text{F}$ to $1600^\circ\text{F}$. This is the ultimate "sweet spot" for wild clay—it is safely past the $1100^\circ\text{F}$ chemical threshold required to turn it into permanent ceramic, but well below the $1900^\circ\text{F}$ meltdown point.

Unless you are actively forcing air into the pit using a leaf blower, hair dryer, or vacuum pipe to turn it into a high-velocity blast furnace, your wood logs alone won't overcook it.

The Visual Thermostat: How to Read the Fire Color

If you want a rough gauge of how hot it is down there at the peak of your burn, look through the gaps in the wood at the glowing coals surrounding the pot:

  • Dull, Dark Red (~$1100^\circ\text{F}$): Just hitting the ceramic transition. Perfect, keep feeding it.
  • Bright Cherry Red (~$1400^\circ\text{F}$): Peak ideal temperature for a wild clay pit-fire.
  • Bright Orange (~$1600^\circ\text{F}$): Getting hot. Stop adding wood and let it coast.
  • Yellow-White ($1800^\circ\text{F}+$): Danger zone for raw surface clay.

Moving to a kiln is a massive upgrade—it gives you precise control over your projects, keeps your work completely clean from ash and soot, and eliminates the physical labor of tending an all-day campfire.

If you want to keep costs as low as possible, your best routes are looking for super cheap second-hand units, building a high-efficiency portable DIY burner, or using free local community resources.

Strategy 1: The "Scavenger" Buy (Used Electric)

You should almost never buy a brand-new electric kiln if you're on a budget. The market is saturated with older, functional electric kilns sitting unused in basements and garages.

  • Where to look: Facebook Marketplace, Craigslist, or local estate auctions. Search terms like "vintage ceramic kiln," "Duncan kiln," "Paragon kiln," or "test kiln."
  • The Price Point: You can frequently find older 120V "test kilns" or small hobby kilns for $50 to $150. People often inherit them, have no idea how to use them, and just want them gone because they are heavy.
  • What to watch out for: * Power requirements: Ensure it runs on a standard 120V household outlet (like a small test kiln). Larger studio kilns require 240V lines (like a clothes dryer outlet), which can limit where you can plug it in.
    • The Coils: Look inside. The heating elements (the metal coils inside the brick grooves) should be intact and not snapped or hanging loose.

Strategy 2: Build a Zero-Cost "Trash Can" Kiln (Gas/Propane)

If you want to build a high-performance kiln for nearly free using scavenged parts, building a top-loading propane fiber-lined kiln is incredibly simple and highly portable.

               [ DIY TRASH CAN KILN ]
               
                  ( Exhaust Hole )
                     |  ||  |
                .____|__||__|____.
                |  ==============  |  <-- Ceramic Fiber Blanket
                | |              | |
                | |   [ POTS ]   | |
                | |              | |
  Burner Port ->| |____      ____| |
  (At Base)     |______\ 🔥 /______|
                        \__/ 
                  (Galvanized Steel Can)

The Materials List:

  1. The Shell: A standard 5-gallon metal bucket or a small 10-gallon galvanized steel trash can (easy to find used or discarded).
  2. The Insulation: A roll of Ceramic Fiber Blanket (like Kaowool). This is the only part you should buy new (around $30–$40 online). It is a flexible, high-temperature wool rated up to $2300^\circ\text{F}$ that lines the inside of the metal can. You pin it to the walls using scrap wire.
  3. The Heat Source: A standard propane weed-burner torch (often found in tool sheds or hardware surplus centers) connected to a standard BBQ propane tank.

How It Works:

You cut a small hole near the bottom edge of the metal can for the torch nozzle to slide into, and a small 3-inch exhaust hole in the lid. The torch blasts a high-velocity flame into the bottom of the can. The flame swirls upward inside the ceramic wool insulation, creating a mini-inferno that easily fires raw wild clay to maturity in just 1 to 2 hours.

Strategy 3: Leverage Community Kilns (Free/Low Cost)

If you don't want to build or store heavy equipment right now, you happen to be in an exceptional area for community kiln access.

  • The Workspace (ISU Memorial Union): They have a fully equipped professional clay studio right on campus with electric kilns fired regularly by staff. While they generally require you to use studio clay for safety reasons, the studio is fully open to the community and provides an incredibly cheap way to work in a pristine environment.
  • The Octagon Center for the Arts (Downtown Ames): They offer open pottery studio access. Often, taking a single entry-level community class gets you long-term access to their studio spaces and kiln firing queues.

turns.prompt_text: We have a public grill at our apartment. I wonder how hot grills can get. Probably not hot enough.
turns.response_html:
You are completely right on both counts—it's a great instinct to look at a public grill as a potential heat source, but a standard apartment charcoal or gas grill will not get hot enough on its own to turn your ravine clay into permanent ceramic.

However, with a tiny bit of "scavenger engineering," you can actually use that public grill as the physical foundation to build a highly effective, temporary mini-kiln.

Here is the breakdown of why the grill alone falls short, and exactly how you can modify it to get the job done safely.

1. Why a Standard Grill Falls Short

To permanently transform your wild clay into a ceramic flower pot, you have to hit that vital $1100^\circ\text{F}$ ($593^\circ\text{C}$) baseline.

  • The Reality of Grills: A standard open-air charcoal or gas apartment grill typically cruises between $350^\circ\text{F}$ and $550^\circ\text{F}$. Even if you completely choke it with charcoal and close the lid, you might max out around $600^\circ\text{F}$ to $700^\circ\text{F}$.
  • The Result: If you put your clay pot inside a standard grill, it will dry out completely and feel stiff, but the second you try to put wet soil or water into it, it will soften and turn right back into mud. It just can't breach that chemical transition temperature.

2. The Solution: The "Grill-Top Charcoal Kiln"

You can use the apartment grill as your safe, legal, and flame-contained workspace, but use a scavenged chimney structure on top of the grate to trap and magnify the heat. This allows you to easily breach $1200^\circ\text{F}$ using simple charcoal.

The Scavenger Materials Needed:

  • The Kiln Shell: A large, empty metal coffee can, a metal popcorn tin, or a cheap galvanized steel bucket.
  • The Insulator: A handful of dry hardwood charcoal briquettes or lump charcoal.
            [ GRILL-TOP MINI-KILN ]
            
                 (Open Top Vent)
                 ._____________.
                 |  [ POT ]    |  <-- Clay pot nested in center
                 |   Charcoal  |  
                 |   Briquettes|  <-- Packed completely around pot
                 |____      ___|
                      | || |       <-- Air intake holes at base
            ===========-======-===========  [ Grill Grate ]
                 ( Active Hot Coals )
            ______________________________  [ Grill Base ]

How to Build and Run It on the Public Grill:

  1. Prep the Metal Can: Take your scavenged metal bucket or large tin and punch 5 or 6 nickel-sized holes around the bottom edge. These act as your air intake vents. Cut the entire top lid off so it is open to the air.
  2. The Charcoal Bed: Light a solid bed of charcoal directly on the apartment grill's lower tray, exactly like you're getting ready to cook burgers. Let them burn until they are glowing red and covered in grey ash.
  3. The Setup: Set your apartment grill grate in place. Put your prepared metal bucket directly on top of the hot grill grate, right over the most intense concentration of coals.
  4. Load the Pot: Put a 2-inch layer of unlit charcoal at the bottom of your bucket. Set your bone-dry clay pot directly on top of that layer, right in the center of the bucket.
  5. The Pack: Pack more unlit charcoal tightly all around the sides of the clay pot, filling the bucket all the way to the rim.

Why This Works:

The intense heat from the grill coals below will rise through the intake holes you punched in the bottom of the bucket, igniting the charcoal packed inside. Because the metal walls of the bucket trap the heat and act as a chimney, the air will draft violently upward. This concentrated airflow turns the inside of the bucket into a high-temperature forge, easily hitting $1200^\circ\text{F}$ to $1400^\circ\text{F}$ right around your pot.

Let it burn completely down until all the charcoal in the bucket turns to ash and cools down naturally. When you dump the ash out, you'll have a fully fired, permanent ceramic piece—all achieved legally and safely on your apartment property.

turns.prompt_text: I'm now wondering what to use as a kiln. A paint bucket sounds like a good night-eve approach, but I don't know how long that will last.
turns.response_html:
You have hit on a really sharp engineering constraint. A standard 5-gallon steel paint bucket or popcorn tin is an excellent "proof-of-concept" shell, but its lifespan is definitely limited.

Because standard sheet steel is very thin, when it is subjected to direct charcoal contact at $1300^\circ\text{F}$, it experiences rapid high-temperature oxidation. The oxygen in the air bonds with the superheated iron, causing the metal to scale, flake, and thin out. A basic paint bucket will usually warp during the first fire and physically burn through or rust out by the third or fourth use.

If you want a scavenged kiln that will last for dozens of fires without costing anything, you need to look for thicker steel, cast iron, or natural ceramics that are built to handle structural heat.

Here are the best long-term, scavenger-friendly alternatives you can look for instead of a paint bucket:

1. The Heavy Steel Brake Drum (The Indestructible Option)

If you want something that will literally last a lifetime and can sit permanently on an apartment grill grate, go to a local auto repair shop or a scrap yard and ask for a discarded cast iron brake drum from a truck or large SUV.

  • Why it works: Brake drums are thick, heavy cast iron designed specifically to absorb and dissipate massive amounts of friction heat without warping or melting.
  • The Setup: Flip it upside down onto the grill grate. The central hub hole acts as a perfect built-in bottom air intake vent. You can stack your charcoal and clay pot right inside the heavy iron bowl. It holds heat beautifully and will never burn through.

2. A Discarded Stainless Steel Stock Pot

Keep an eye out at garage sales, thrift stores, or apartment dumpster enclosures for a large, heavy-duty stainless steel cooking pot or a dented stock pot.

  • Why it works: Stainless steel contains chromium and nickel, which form a protective oxide layer that resists high-temperature scaling incredibly well. It can withstand charcoal fire temperatures much longer than plain regular steel, giving you dozens of successful firings before it degrades.

3. Terracotta-on-Terracotta (The Natural Kiln)

Instead of metal, you can use a large, cheap, or cracked terracotta flower pot flipped upside down as your kiln shell on top of the grill.

  • Why it works: Terracotta is already a fired ceramic. It doesn't care about the heat of a charcoal fire because it was born in one. It won't rust, scale, or burn through.
  • The Setup: Set your clay piece and charcoal on the grill, and place a large, inverted terracotta pot directly over them like a dome. The drainage hole at the top of the flower pot acts as the perfect exhaust chimney for the rising heat.

The Verdict for Your Project

If you just want to see if your ravine clay actually vitrifies and turns into a real ceramic pot this week, go ahead and use a basic paint bucket or large tin can. Treat it as a disposable tool just to test your method.

Once you prove the process works, upgrading to a heavy cast-iron brake drum or a large terracotta dome will give you a permanent, highly reliable scavenger setup for all your future casting and spine-modeling projects.
